_meta.purpose: Business-model archetypes with notes on where each has actually worked and why. Used by the agent to match an idea to a model that fits the culture and resource level.
_meta.warning: Archetypes are priors, not rules. Use them to generate tests, never as conclusions.

patterns.name: Build the trust rail first
patterns.essence: In markets with low institutional trust, whoever builds escrow, verified reviews, guaranteed refunds or certified identity owns the market.
worked_where: Alipay + Wangwang in China (eBay lacked it)
failed_where: eBay China - listed fees without solving trust
US-imported 'anonymous' transaction models in cash economies
signals_you_need_it: Target market scores high on uncertainty avoidance
Cash-on-delivery or cash-first payments are normal
Formal contracts are weakly enforced
Customers ask 'who are you?' before 'how much?'
patterns.first_test: Run 10 transactions manually with a human guarantee and see if strangers will pay.

patterns.name: Formalise what already exists informally
patterns.essence: Do not create new supply or new behaviour - organise existing informal supply (drivers, home cooks, tailors, tutors) and give it identity, payments and demand.
failed_where: Platforms that demanded exclusivity or asset purchase from informal workers
Models requiring workers to buy equipment upfront
signals_you_need_it: Large informal sector in target market
Existing work happening off-books
No formal credit or identity for those workers
patterns.first_test: Recruit 20 existing informal providers and give them a simple booking channel. Do they bring their own customers?

patterns.name: Razor-blade / consumables annuity
patterns.essence: Sell the durable asset cheaply (or at cost) and make money on recurring consumables.
worked_where: Printers, coffee capsules, M-Pesa agent float, Apple's app+services ecosystem, subscription supplements in the US
failed_where: Juicero (workaround existed)
Pets.com (delivery cost exceeded recurring margin)
Products where the customer can substitute a generic consumable easily
signals_you_need_it: You can lock the consumable (format, licence, chemistry)
The customer uses the product repeatedly and predictably
Shipping cost per consumable is low relative to margin
patterns.first_test: Check whether a 3rd-party consumable already exists on Amazon/Shopee for your category. If yes, your lock-in is imaginary.

patterns.name: Social collateral instead of financial collateral
patterns.essence: Use group guarantee, community reputation and peer accountability where people have no credit history or assets.
worked_where: Grameen Bank and microfinance in Bangladesh/India
Rotating savings associations (chit funds, chama, susu, biao hui)
Chinese and Jewish diaspora trade networks
failed_where: Commercialised microfinance without the community layer - led to over-indebtedness
Group models in anonymous urban settings with no social ties
signals_you_need_it: No formal credit bureau coverage
Strong existing group structures (village, church, clan, immigrant community)
Trust is personal, not institutional
patterns.first_test: Ask 5 people in the target community who they would trust to vouch for a stranger's repayment.

patterns.name: Local champion against a global giant
patterns.essence: Beat an incoming global brand on local taste, density, price point and relationships before it localises.
worked_where: Local banks vs global banks in Africa/Middle East
failed_where: Mimicking the global player's positioning instead of owning the local one
Local champions that lost the price war to subsidised entrants
signals_you_need_it: A global player is entering or eyeing your market
Your product has a culturally specific taste/format that the giant's global SKU cannot match
You can add store density or delivery density faster than they can
patterns.first_test: Find the one thing your local market prefers that the global playbook would never authorise. Build that only.

patterns.name: Serve the long tail the giants ignore
patterns.essence: Global platforms serve the head of the market (big brands, big merchants, big enterprise). Serving the millions of tiny operators is a durable business.
failed_where: Chasing the tail with an enterprise cost structure
Underestimating support cost per tiny customer
signals_you_need_it: Huge number of self-employed/micro businesses in your target market
Incumbents priced for enterprises
Distribution can happen online or through community channels
patterns.first_test: Can you acquire 100 tiny customers with zero sales headcount? If not, the tail model will not work for you yet.

patterns.name: Cluster / network-based production
patterns.essence: Use many small specialised players linked by trust instead of one big vertically integrated factory.
worked_where: Indian textile and jewellery clusters in Surat, Tiruppur
failed_where: When competition shifts to scale, brand and capex-heavy technology
When the cluster cannot solve succession or marketing
signals_you_need_it: You are in a craft or high-mix manufacturing category
Many small suppliers already exist locally
Speed-to-design matters more than unit cost
patterns.first_test: Map 10 suppliers in your target cluster and see if you can assemble the full chain without owning any of it.

patterns.name: Family-firm and relationship contracting
patterns.essence: Long-term personal relationships replace legal contracts; reputation across generations is the enforcement mechanism.
failed_where: Outsiders trying to transact with family networks on price alone
Any model requiring rapid hostile restructuring
signals_you_need_it: High power distance + collectivism in the target market
Supplier relationships are decades long
Price alone does not win the deal
patterns.first_test: Ask whether you can name the actual decision-maker's family or community connection before pitching. If not, your sales cycle is not ready.

patterns.name: Leapfrog the missing infrastructure
patterns.essence: When a market skipped a technology generation, design for the state it is actually in - mobile-only, cash-and-mobile-money, offline-first - rather than assuming the rich-world stack.
worked_where: WhatsApp commerce in Brazil and India
Mobile-first e-commerce in Indonesia and Africa
failed_where: Products requiring desktop, card payment or stable broadband
Apps assuming English literacy
signals_you_need_it: Low card penetration, high mobile penetration
Poor fixed-line or logistics infrastructure
'Legacy-free' market that never had the previous generation
patterns.first_test: Can your product complete its core task on a $60 Android phone with 2GB RAM, spotty 3G and cash? If not, redesign.

patterns.name: Community and social-commerce distribution
patterns.essence: Sell through trusted community members (resellers, agents, community leaders, group chats) instead of mass advertising.
worked_where: WeChat group commerce and buying agents
failed_where: Pyramid structures that consume the reseller's own social capital
When inventory risk is pushed onto the reseller
signals_you_need_it: High collectivism and dense social networks
Advertising trust is low, word-of-mouth trust is high
Sparse retail coverage in the target geography
patterns.first_test: Give 10 community members a product to sell to their own group. Measure re-order within 30 days.

patterns.name: Asset-light supply arbitrage
patterns.essence: Aggregate other people's assets or idle capacity instead of buying your own.
worked_where: Airbnb, Uber, Instacart vs Webvan's warehouses
Cloud kitchens in India and SEA
failed_where: WeWork (long leases = assets on balance sheet anyway)
Marketplaces where quality control becomes impossible without ownership
signals_you_need_it: Idle capacity exists and is easy to enumerate
Quality can be standardised through process rather than ownership
Capital is expensive to you
patterns.first_test: Can you fulfil your first 20 orders without owning anything? If yes, stay asset-light until density forces otherwise.

patterns.name: Regulated-first market entry
patterns.essence: In high-uncertainty-avoidance markets, certification, licensing and compliance are marketing assets, not costs.
worked_where: German Mittelstand B2B and certification culture
Halal certification as a market-access unlock across SEA, Gulf and Muslim markets
failed_where: Ignoring local licensing until after launch
Assuming a licence in one jurisdiction works in another
signals_you_need_it: Target market scores high on uncertainty avoidance
Heavy product regulation (food, health, finance, children's products)
Religious or cultural certification requirements
patterns.first_test: List every licence/certification required and estimate the cost and time before building anything.

patterns.name: Localise the menu, keep the brand
patterns.essence: The brand can travel; the recipe, price point and packaging must be rebuilt per market.
worked_where: Coca-Cola keeping Thums Up in India
failed_where: Walmart in Germany (operating norms, not menu)
Global retailers assuming pricing power travels
Brands that killed acquired local favourites
signals_you_need_it: Food, beverage, retail or consumer packaged goods
Your home market is not your target market
Religious, dietary or taste norms differ
patterns.first_test: Take your top 3 products to 20 local consumers and ask which one they would replace an existing habit with. If none, rebuild the lineup.

patterns.name: Patient capital / long-horizon structures
patterns.essence: Structures that let you hold assets and relationships through cycles beat structures forced to exit quarterly.
worked_where: Family offices in Italy and the Gulf
failed_where: Patient capital becomes complacent capital
Structures with no external discipline drift into bad investments
signals_you_need_it: Your market has decade-long payback cycles (infrastructure, manufacturing, brand building)
Public markets would punish your investment schedule
You can access capital not subject to quarterly redemption
patterns.first_test: Work out what your idea looks like if it takes 7 years. If it only works in 18 months, your capital structure is your real constraint.
